Content:
Let's recall some definitions for sequences with infinite limits:

Content:
The notation
[MATH: \lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = \infty]
has the following definition:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: M > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] we have [MATH: a_n \gt M.]

Content:
The essence of this definition is captured in the image shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ebf8a28bf5efa61322b513a11a1d63dc]

Content:
Similarly, the notation
[MATH: \lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = -\infty]
has the following definition:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: M < 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] we have [MATH: a_n \lt M.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4b2266bddaace15f839bd564bfbdc8fc]

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to prove that a sequence has an infinite limit.

Content:
Constructing a proof that a sequence has an infinite limit mostly boils down to finding a suitable [MATH: N(M)] that satisfies one of the definitions above. So, let's get some practice with that first.

Note that this sequence is divergent:

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, notice that [MATH: 2\sqrt[3]{n}- 3 > 0] for any natural [MATH: n \geq 4.]

So, we solve the inequality [MATH: a_n > M] for [MATH: n \geq 4{:}]

[MATH: 2root(n, 3) − 3|> M; 2root(n, 3)|> M + 3; root(n, 3)|> (M + 3)/(2); n|> ((M + 3)^{3})/(8)]

Then, we let [MATH: N] be the smallest natural number such that

[MATH: N > \dfrac{(M+3)^3}{8}.]

Notice that, since [MATH: M > 0,] we have that [MATH: ((M + 3)^{3})/(8)|> (3^{3})/(8); > (27)/(8); > 3]

and therefore [MATH: N \geq 4.]

Therefore, [MATH: 2\sqrt[3]{n}- 3 > M] for all natural numbers [MATH: n \geq N.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's recall some definitions for sequences with infinite limits:

Content:
The notation
[MATH: \lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = \infty]
has the following definition:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: M > 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] we have [MATH: a_n \gt M.]

Content:
The essence of this definition is captured in the image shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ebf8a28bf5efa61322b513a11a1d63dc]

Content:
Similarly, the notation
[MATH: \lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = -\infty]
has the following definition:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: M < 0] there exists a natural number [MATH: N] such that for every natural number [MATH: n \geq N,] we have [MATH: a_n \lt M.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4b2266bddaace15f839bd564bfbdc8fc]

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to prove that a sequence has an infinite limit.

Content:
Constructing a proof that a sequence has an infinite limit mostly boils down to finding a suitable [MATH: N(M)] that satisfies one of the definitions above. So, let's get some practice with that first.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Finding a Suitable N

Content:
Consider the following sequence:

Content:
[MATH: a_n = 2\sqrt{n}, \qquad n \geq 1]

Content:
Note that this sequence is divergent:
[MATH: \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(2\sqrt n\right) = \infty]

Content:
Given that [MATH: M > 0,] let's find a natural number [MATH: N(M)] such that for all [MATH: n \geq N,] we have

Content:
[MATH: a_n > M.]

Content:
First, we solve the inequality [MATH: a_n > M] for [MATH: n{:}]

Content:
[MATH: 2sqrt(n)|> M; sqrt(n)|> (M)/(2); n|> ((M)/(2))^{2}; n|> (M^{2})/(4)]

Content:
So, we let [MATH: N] be the smallest natural number such that

Content:
[MATH: N > \dfrac{M^2}{4}.]

Content:
And that's it! Given any [MATH: M >0,] no matter how large, [MATH: a_n] is guaranteed to be larger than [MATH: M] provided that [MATH: n\geq N,] where [MATH: N] is the smallest natural number larger than [MATH: \dfrac{M^2}{4}.]

Therefore, [MATH: 1-3n < M] for all natural numbers [MATH: n \geq N.]
